The real default path was also verified manually: with the repo's own `.env`, `rm -f cms.db; uv run python scripts/seed_demo.py` exits 0 (before the fix, exit 1).\n448\t- `cms serve` not verified: **Resolved.** Started `uv run cms serve --port 8123` and `GET /login` returned 200.\n449\t- Scope creep (`export` prefix, quote stripping): **Accepted**, a few lines and standard `.env` syntax.\n450\t- `CMS_DATABASE=cms.db` is relative to cwd: **Accepted**; the grader runs all steps from the repo root, and the test relies on cwd semantics.\n451\t- Unrelated `notes/usage-ledger.csv` change: **Excluded** from this commit.\n452\t\n453\tResult: 115 tests pass; new test fails without the fix.\n454\t\n455\t"}]},"uuid":"9ffa9ff8-f800-4eeb-9510-10f766693dea","timestamp":"2026-10-15T13:57:37.117Z","toolUseResult":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/Users/biswas1/.claude/projects/-Users-biswas1-code-iphs400-mp2-cms/9c18cc4d-d420-4c1a-83a4-349b624f72ef/tool-results/b411ooydj.txt","content":"=================== # 1 Spec: KCFC web CMS\n## Problem Statement\n\nThe Kenyon College Finance Club (KCFC) is run by three Presidents and about eight Officers, and nearly everything is communicated by email to financeclub@kenyon.edu. The current Wix site shows no officers, no meeting time and no events, its Contact Us link goes back to the homepage, and its Resources headings have nothing under them, so a first-year or an alumnus can reasonably conclude the club is dead. Only one or two people can update it, there is no way to give Officers limited access, and nothing stops an unfinished stock pitch from going out under the club's name in front of William Blair alumni. When leadership changes there is no clean way to hand over or take away access.\n\nVocabulary below is defined in `CONTEXT.md`.\n\n## Users\n\n- **Presidents** (3, Admin role): run the club, review everything, sign off on what goes public.\n- **Officers** (about 8, Editor role): contribute meeting announcements, pitch writeups and alumni call recaps. Not technical; an announcement must take under two minutes.\n- **Visitors** (never log in): prospective members (first-years and sophomores) asking \"what is this, do I need experience, when and where do you meet\"; current members looking for event details, the resume review form and the Analyst Program; alumni and recruiters (including William Blair) checking leadership and activity before an event or pitch review.\n\n## Solution\n\nA small CMS with a local admin console on the Club laptop and a static public site. Presidents and Officers sign in with individual accounts. Officers write Posts and save Drafts; only Presidents publish, manage Pages, and manage Users. A Publish run turns everything Published into a static site on GitHub Pages. The first thing a Visitor sees is the next meeting. Nothing unreviewed reaches the public site, and an Officer who leaves loses access without anyone changing a shared password.\n\n## The 7 required capabilities, in KCFC's words\n\n1. **Login.** Presidents and Officers sign in and out with their Kenyon email and their own password. Passwords are stored hashed, never as text. A President sets the first password face to face, and resets lost passwords in person. Signed in on the shared Club laptop, a User is signed out after about 2 hours idle.\n2. **Two roles.** *Admin* (the three Presidents) can do everything. *Editor* (Officers) can write and edit only their own Posts, save them as Drafts and delete their own Drafts. An Editor cannot publish, cannot delete a Published Post, cannot touch any Page, and cannot see user management. These limits are enforced by the system itself, including when an Editor types a restricted address straight into the browser (the WordPress \"Editor can trash the About page\" problem from the field notes).\n3. **Posts.** One kind of Post (meeting announcement, pitch writeup, or alumni call recap), no categories. Each has a title, slug, Markdown body, Draft/Published status, author and timestamps, and can be created, read, updated and deleted under the role rules above. The slug is made from the title once and never changes when the title is edited; only an Admin can edit it. An Editor's edit to a Published Post turns it back into a Draft until a President republishes it. An Admin's edit leaves it Published.\n4. **Pages.** Lasting club information: Homepage, About, Leadership, Analyst Program, Join (for prospective members), Recruiting (for current members: resume review form link, standing guides). Same fields as a Post, but only Admins may create, edit, or delete them. Published Pages appear in the public Navigation in an order an Admin sets. The Homepage opens with the **next-meeting line** (plain text such as \"Next meeting: Wed Oct 28, 7 pm, Oden 110\", updated by a President the night before), then the contact email, then the latest Posts.\n5. **Admin console.** A dashboard with counts of Drafts, Published items and Pending changes (Admins also see active and Deactivated User counts), a one-click \"New Post\" button, and a \"pending changes\" banner so nobody assumes saved work is already Live. A content list, newest first, filterable by status (All / Published / Draft, with counts) and type; Editors see only their own Posts. An editor with a side-by-side Preview of the sanitized Markdown, labelled \"Draft, not Live\" when it is not.\n6. **User management (Admin only).** Presidents create Users, change Roles, and Deactivate Users. A Deactivated User cannot sign in, and an open session ends at their next action. Users are never deleted: when seniors graduate in May their old Posts keep their name but they cannot log in. A Deactivated User can be reactivated. At least one President must always stay active, and a President cannot deactivate themselves.\n7. **Public site and publish.** Visitors see only Published content. Markdown is sanitized (see below). Navigation is built from Published Pages plus a link to the Posts listing (newest first, title and date). Each Post shows a byline, \"By <name>, <date>\", never an email address; Pages show none. `cms publish` (Admin only, usually run right before a meeting) writes `site/` with relative paths only and deploys it to GitHub Pages. Marking an item Published has a \"Publish this?\" confirm. There is no change summary; a mistake is fixed by unpublishing and running it again.\n\n## User Stories\n\n1. As a first-year, I want the next meeting's date, time and place at the very top of the homepage, so that I know when and where to show up.\n2. As a prospective member, I want a Join page saying what the club does and whether I need experience, so that I can decide whether to come.\n3. As a prospective member, I want the contact email on the homepage, so that I can ask a question.\n4. As a current member, I want a Recruiting page with the resume review form link, so that I can request a review without digging through email.\n5. As a current member, I want a list of Posts, newest first, so that I can find the latest announcement.\n6. As a current member, I want to read about the Analyst Program on its own page, so that I know what it involves.\n7. As an alumnus, I want a Leadership page, so that I know who runs the club before I speak at an event.\n8. As a recruiter or William Blair alumnus, I want to read reviewed pitch writeups and recaps, so that I can see the club's work, and I want to see only reviewed work.\n9. As a Visitor, I want links that keep working, so that a shared link to a Post is never dead.\n10. As a Visitor, I want to see an author's name but never their email address, so that student contact details stay private.\n11. As a Visitor, I want the site to work when served from a GitHub Pages subfolder, so that no page or link is broken.\n12. As an Officer, I want my own account, so that I never share a password.\n13. As an Officer, I want to sign in with my Kenyon email, so that it is easy to remember.\n14. As an Officer, I want to write a meeting announcement in under two minutes, so that updating the site is not a chore.\n15. As an Officer, I want to write in plain Markdown with a preview beside it, so that I can see what the Post will look like.\n16. As an Officer, I want to save my work as a Draft, so that I can finish it later.\n17. As an Officer, I want my Draft to stay private until a President publishes it, so that nothing goes public by accident.\n18. As an Officer, I want to see and edit only my own Posts, so that I do not break another team's pitch before the William Blair presentation.\n19. As an Officer, I want to delete my own abandoned Drafts, so that my list stays clean.\n20. As an Officer, I want to be told clearly when I cannot do something, so that I do not think the site is broken.\n21. As an Officer, I want a \"Draft, not Live\" label on my preview, so that I do not think members can already see it.\n22. As an Officer, I want to be signed out automatically on the shared laptop, so that the next person cannot use my account.\n23. As an Officer, I want my name on my Post after I graduate, so that my work keeps its credit.\n24. As a President, I want to review every Draft in one list, so that I can sign off before publishing.\n25. As a President, I want to see all Drafts filtered by status with counts, so that I know what still needs attention.\n26. As a President, I want to edit any Post, so that I can fix a pitch writeup before it goes out.\n27. As a President, I want an Officer's edit to a Published Post to turn it back to Draft, so that no unreviewed change goes out.\n28. As a President, I want a \"Publish this?\" confirm, so that I do not publish by mis-click.\n29. As a President, I want to unpublish a Post or Page, so that I can take down a mistake and rerun the publish.\n30. As a President, I want to delete a Post or Page after an \"are you sure?\" step, so that deletion is deliberate.\n31. As a President, I want only Presidents to edit or delete Leadership and Analyst Program (and every other Page), so that Officers cannot damage official pages.\n32. As a President, I want to set the order of Pages in Navigation, so that the menu reads sensibly.\n33. As a President, I want to edit the Homepage's next-meeting line, so that the first thing a first-year sees is current.\n34. As a President, I want a banner showing pending changes, so that I know the live site is behind.\n35. As a President, I want to run `cms publish` right before a meeting, so that the public site is up to date.\n36. As a President, I want to create accounts and set the first password in person, so that no email system is required.\n37. As a President, I want to reset a lost password in person, so that Officers are never locked out.\n38. As a President, I want to change a User's role, so that a new President can be made Admin at turnover.\n39. As a President, I want to deactivate an outgoing Officer, so that they can no longer sign in.\n40. As a President, I want a deactivated User to lose access immediately, even if signed in, so that handover is clean.\n41. As a President, I want to reactivate a User, so that a returning Officer does not need a new account.\n42. As a President, I want the system to refuse to deactivate the last active President or myself, so that the club cannot lock itself out.\n43. As a President, I want an Editor who types an Admin address into the browser to be refused, so that restrictions are real and not just hidden menu items.\n44. As a President, I want dashboard counts, so that I can see the state of the site at a glance.\n45. As a President, I want Posts to keep their author when the user is Deactivated, so that the archive stays accurate.\n46. As a President, I want Markdown to be sanitized everywhere it renders, so that nobody can inject a script into the club's site.\n47. As a President, I want the database file never to be committed, so that accounts and Drafts stay private.\n48. As a President, I want to hand the whole system to next year's Presidents without a shared password, so that continuity does not depend on one person.\n\n## Implementation Decisions\n\n- **Architecture** follows ADR-001 (admin console local, public site static, explicit publish) and ADR-002 (FastAPI + Jinja + SQLite, argon2, no frontend framework). The dependency set in `pyproject.toml` is fixed; adding any dependency needs asking first.\n- **Roles:** exactly two, Admin and Editor. Permission checks live in one place on the server and every admin route goes through it, so direct URL access is refused as reliably as hidden menus. Editor-restricted requests return a refusal or redirect, never the page.\n- **Content model:** Post and Page share fields (title, slug, Markdown body, status Draft/Published, author, created and updated timestamps). A Post has no kind or category. Pages additionally have a navigation order. Status for a Page is Draft or Published like a Post.\n- **Slug rules:** generated from the title on first save, unique, immutable on title edit, editable only by an Admin, no redirects from old slugs. Navigation and the Posts listing use slugs, so links stay stable.\n- **Editing rules:** an Editor can read and change only Posts they authored; an Editor's save on a Published Post sets it to Draft. An Admin's save keeps its status. Marking Published is Admin-only and goes through a \"Publish this?\" confirm.\n- **Delete rules:** Admin can delete any Post or Page after a confirm step; an Editor can delete only their own Drafts. Unpublish (return to Draft) is separate from delete.\n- **Users:** email and argon2-hashed password; roles; active flag. Deactivating sets the flag; every request checks it, so an open session is refused at the next action. Users are never deleted. Guard rails: cannot deactivate or demote yourself, the last active Admin cannot be deactivated or demoted. First password is set by an Admin; no forced change at first sign-in; no email-based reset. Sessions are signed cookies with an idle timeout of about 2 hours.\n- **CSRF:** every state-changing form carries a CSRF token.\n- **Sanitizing:** every rendered body goes through the sanitizer, both in the admin Preview and in the exported site. Scripts, event handlers such as `onerror`, iframes and `javascript:` links are stripped. Plain formatting, headings, lists and normal links stay. Raw HTML embeds are not supported and images are out of scope.\n- **Publish:** the exporter renders only Published Posts and Pages into `site/` using relative paths only (never `href=\"/...\"` or `src=\"/...\"`): Homepage (with the next-meeting line and latest Posts), each Page, the Posts listing, each Post with its byline, and Navigation built from Published Pages in Admin-set order plus the Posts listing. Drafts never leave the database. `site/` is generated, never hand-edited. Deployment pushes `site/` to the `gh-pages` branch. \"Pending changes\" is the difference between current Published content and what the last Publish run wrote.\n- **Console screens:** login/logout, dashboard (counts, New Post, pending changes banner), content list with status and type filters and counts, editor with side-by-side Preview, Page ordering, user management (Admin only).\n- **Seed and demo:** the existing seed script builds a demo database with one Admin and one Editor.\n\n## Testing Decisions\n\n- A good test checks external behaviour only: what a signed-in role sees, can do, and is refused, and what ends up in the generated site. It does not assert on internal functions or database layout.\n- **Seam 1, the HTTP app,** through the existing `client` and `client_as(\"admin\" | \"editor\")` fixtures. This covers login and logout, role permissions (including direct URL access), Post/Page CRUD, slug immutability, Editor-edit-reverts-to-Draft, own-Drafts-only, deactivation, last-Admin and self-deactivation guards, CSRF rejection, idle timeout, dashboard counts, filters and preview.\n- **Seam 2, the site export,** through the existing render function (`render_site(out_dir)`). It covers only-Published content, Drafts absent, sanitizer behaviour (scripts, `onerror`, iframes, `javascript:` links stripped; headings, lists, links kept), navigation order, byline text with no email, and no root-absolute `href`/`src`.\n- No new seams are needed; these two already exist and are the highest available. The seed should load `.env` itself and succeed with the `.env.example` values.\n\n## Cause (confirmed)\nNothing in the app or `scripts/seed_demo.py` reads `.env`. `uv run` does not load it (no `--env-file`), and the script only checks `os.environ`, which is empty unless the user exported the variables by hand. `app/settings.py` has the same gap, so `cms serve` also ignores `.env` (CMS_DATABASE, CMS_SITE_TITLE, CMS_SECRET_KEY).\n\n## Fix plan\n- Load `.env` (stdlib-only parser, no new dependency) in `app/settings.py` before settings are read; real environment variables win over `.env`.\n- Add a test that runs the seed script as a subprocess from a fresh copy of `.env.example`.\n---- COMMENT 2026-10-15T04:27:25Z\n## /code-review findings (Standards + Spec, run in parallel) and resolutions\n\n### Standards\n- **No hard violations.** Stdlib-only parser (no new dependency), no secret/password logged, `.env`/`*.db` stay gitignored, test uses a tmp copy of `.env.example`.\n- Judgement: loader had no unit tests (quotes, `export`, comments, `=` in value). **Resolved:** added `test_load_env_file_parses_and_real_environment_wins` and `test_load_env_file_missing_file_is_fine`.\n- Smell, Speculative Generality: `CMS_ENV_FILE` comment mentioned \"odd deployments\". **Resolved:** comment reworded; the knob exists only so the test suite can use a scratch copy of `.env.example`.\n- Smell, Divergent Change (parser lives in `settings.py`): **Accepted.** Small and deliberate; settings must load `.env` before it reads any value.\n- Temporal coupling in `seed_demo.py` (settings import must precede the `os.environ` check): **Accepted**, commented in code.\n- Inline `# comment` after a value stays in the value: **Accepted**; `.env.example` has none.\n\n### Spec\n- Subprocess test bypasses the default `ROOT/.env` lookup via `CMS_ENV_FILE`. **Resolved in part:** added `test_default_env_file_is_dot_env_at_repo_root`. The real default path was also verified manually: with the repo's own `.env`, `rm -f cms.db; uv run python scripts/seed_demo.py` exits 0 (before the fix, exit 1).\n- `cms serve` not verified: **Resolved.** Started `uv run cms serve --port 8123` and `GET /login` returned 200.\n- Scope creep (`export` prefix, quote stripping): **Accepted**, a few lines and standard `.env` syntax.\n- `CMS_DATABASE=cms.db` is relative to cwd: **Accepted**; the grader runs all steps from the repo root, and the test relies on cwd semantics.\n- Unrelated `notes/usage-ledger.csv` change: **Excluded** from this commit.\n\nResult: 115 tests pass; new test fails without the fix.\n\n","numLines":455,"startLine":1,"totalLines":455}},"sourceToolAssistantUUID":"06504684-ee6b-44b4-989a-462c4002a658","permissionDecision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reasonType":"mode"},"session_id":"9c18cc4d-d420-4c1a-83a4-349b624f72ef","userType":"external","entrypoint":"cli","cwd":"/Users/biswas1/code/iphs400-mp2-cms","sessionId":"9c18cc4d-d420-4c1a-83a4-349b624f72ef","version":"2.1.300","gitBranch":"main"}

{"type":"api-request-blob","sessionId":"9c18cc4d-d420-4c1a-83a4-349b624f72ef","hash":"a27e8befa6a00231db14cf56574c13e9abba7f1a177bb19ab5711a3c644c98e1","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"tool_result","content":"Exit code 1\n     1\t# IPHS 400 MP2 Report: A CMS for the Kenyon College Finance Club\n     2\t\n     3\t**Aishik Biswas · October 15, 2026**  \n     4\t**Repository:** [GitHub](https://github.com/iaishikb-rgb/iphs400-mp2-cms) · **Live site:** [Finance Club CMS](https://iaishikb-rgb.github.io/iphs400-mp2-cms/)\n     5\t\n     6\t## 1. What I built, and which decisions were mine\n     7\t\n     8\tI built a small CMS for the Kenyon College Finance Club, which I run alongside my two co-presidents, Lucas Flynn and Madeline Ha. Our current Wix website does not adequately represent the club’s activities. It lists no current officers or meeting times, its “Contact Us” link leads back to the homepage, and a Wix advertising banner appears across the top. For an alumnus visiting the website, this could suggest that the club is no longer active. Most of our information is communicated through club emails, which means members often have to search earlier messages for basic details, including our meetings every other week in Oden 110.\n     9\t\n    10\tThe CMS provides a local admin console built with FastAPI and SQLite, where Presidents and Officers can sign in, write Posts and Pages in Markdown, and preview their work. The `cms publish` command generates a static site from Live content for publication on GitHub Pages. Presidents have administrator access, while Officers have editor access. The implementation covers all seven required capabilities, with 123 tests in the final suite.\n    11\t\n    12\tSeveral decisions emerged from my responses to the grill, particularly where I changed or rejected Claude’s recommendations:\n    13\t\n    14\t- **No required password change at first sign-in.** Claude proposed this additional step, but I decided it was unnecessary for our setup. There are approximately eight officers, and a President sets each password face to face. Given the deadline, I did not think another screen was justified. I retained a two-hour idle sign-out because we share a laptop during meetings.\n    15\t- **Only Presidents can publish.** Officers can prepare drafts, but publication requires a President. In the spring, our three sector teams present stock pitches to Kenyon alumni working at William Blair. Material published under the club’s name should therefore be complete and reviewed.\n    16\t- **Only Presidents can manage Pages.** This decision came directly from my sixth WordPress field note, where I found that an Editor could move the About page to the trash. Officers contributing announcements should not also have control over official pages such as Leadership and the Analyst Program.\n    17\t- **Publishing uses a simple confirmation.** Claude suggested displaying a summary of changes before every publish run. I chose a straightforward “Publish this?” confirmation, with the option to unpublish content and run the command again if a correction is needed.\n    18\t- **Pitch writeups credit teams in the body text.** I decided against adding a separate team field. The byline identifies whoever posted the writeup, while the text credits the members who contributed.\n    19\t- **The next meeting appears as a manually edited line on the Homepage.** I chose this over automatic date logic because one of us already updates the email reminder before each meeting. Updating the website can follow the same routine.\n    20\t\n    21\t## 2. Where the AI drifted, and what caught it\n    22\t\n    23\tThe clearest problem was an explicitly requested fix that Claude reported as complete without resolving it. In my T07 prompt, I explained that `scripts/seed_demo.py` would not run with a fresh `.env` file and displayed “Set CMS_ADMIN_PASSWORD and CMS_EDITOR_PASSWORD in .env.” I asked Claude to fix the issue and add a test. It subsequently reported T07 as complete, with all 111 tests passing.\n    24\t\n    25\tHowever, when I ran the seed script myself at approximately 12:20 a.m., it produced the same error and exited, preventing the server from starting. None of the unit tests actually ran the script, which explains why the suite passed. I discovered the problem while manually trying to use the app. I then opened bug issue #9 and addressed it with a test that runs the seed script as a subprocess using a fresh copy of `.env.example`.\n    26\t\n    27\tOther departures from the specification were identified through `/code-review`:\n    28\t\n    29\t- **T01: conflicting glossary files.** The installed skills were newer than those described in the manual and expected a `GLOSSARY.md` file. Although I had already specified in `CLAUDE.md` that the glossary belonged in `CONTEXT.md`, an empty `GLOSSARY.md` and a reference to it in `docs/agents/domain.md` still appeared. The review identified this contradiction, which I corrected in commit `1557b24`. Leaving it unresolved could have caused later tickets to rely on different sources for the project’s vocabulary.\n    30\t- **T06: President self-demotion.** The initial user management implementation allowed a President to demote themselves, despite the specification prohibiting this. With three co-presidents managing accounts, this seemed like a plausible mistake during the spring leadership transition. The review caught it before the commit.\n    31\t- **T05: an addition I retained.** Claude included Pages in the dashboard counts even though the ticket did not request this. I kept the addition because it helps the Presidents identify unpublished pages.\n    32\t\n    33\t## 3. Skills, prompts, and resources\n    34\t\n    35\tI followed the sequence `/grill-with-docs`, `/to-spec`, and `/to-tickets`, which produced seven tickets corresponding to issues #2–#8. I then used `/implement` for each ticket, which invoked `/tdd`, followed by `/code-review`.\n    36\t\n    37\tThe grill was the most useful part of the process. Its 18 questions required me to make specific decisions about how the CMS should serve the club, including the choices described above. The review stage was also valuable because it identified problems in work that `/implement` had already reported as finished.\n    38\t\n    39\tOne source of confusion was the difference between ticket labels and GitHub issue numbers. Since the specification occupied issue #1, tickets T01–T07 corresponded to issues #2–#8. When I first entered `/implement #3`, Claude asked whether I meant T02 or T03. After that, I included both identifiers, such as `/implement #4 (T03)`.\n    40\t\n    41\tI also used WordPress Playground for the field trip, the manual and rubric in the starter repository, and the club’s existing Wix website for background information. Since I had not used Orca or this workflow before, I kept a separate Claude conversation open for guidance on terminal commands and Git steps.\n    42\t\n    43\t## 4. Budget, next steps, and reflections\n    44\t\n    45\tThe following figures come from `notes/usage-ledger.csv`, processed through `scripts/usage_report.py`.\n    46\t\n    47\t| Stage | Planned usage | Actual usage |\n    48\t| --- | --- | --- |\n    49\t| Grill, specification, and tickets | 35% of a five-hour window using opusplan | 3% using Sonnet |\n    50\t| Implementation and review per ticket | Approximately 20% | 1–7%, averaging approximately 3% |\n    51\t| All seven tickets | Approximately 140% | 22% |\n    52\t| Weekly cap | Estimated at 25–35% | Approximately 5% |\n    53\t\n    54\tMy estimate for the seven tickets was roughly six times the recorded usage. Switching the planning stages from opusplan to Sonnet and using `/clear` between tickets likely contributed to the lower usage. {"parentUuid":"299bc497-efd4-4ecb-b0dc-01b521c6b556","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"9acc77cd-1d7b-4777-a4f0-bd06dabcb5ef","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"tool_result","content":"Exit code 1\n     1\t# IPHS 400 MP2 Report: A CMS for the Kenyon College Finance Club\n     2\t\n     3\t**Aishik Biswas · October 15, 2026**  \n     4\t**Repository:** [GitHub](https://github.com/iaishikb-rgb/iphs400-mp2-cms) · **Live site:** [Finance Club CMS](https://iaishikb-rgb.github.io/iphs400-mp2-cms/)\n     5\t\n     6\t## 1. What I built, and which decisions were mine\n     7\t\n     8\tI built a small CMS for the Kenyon College Finance Club, which I run alongside my two co-presidents, Lucas Flynn and Madeline Ha. Our current Wix website does not adequately represent the club’s activities. It lists no current officers or meeting times, its “Contact Us” link leads back to the homepage, and a Wix advertising banner appears across the top. For an alumnus visiting the website, this could suggest that the club is no longer active. Most of our information is communicated through club emails, which means members often have to search earlier messages for basic details, including our meetings every other week in Oden 110.\n     9\t\n    10\tThe CMS provides a local admin console built with FastAPI and SQLite, where Presidents and Officers can sign in, write Posts and Pages in Markdown, and preview their work. The `cms publish` command generates a static site from Live content for publication on GitHub Pages. Presidents have administrator access, while Officers have editor access. The implementation covers all seven required capabilities, with 123 tests in the final suite.\n    11\t\n    12\tSeveral decisions emerged from my responses to the grill, particularly where I changed or rejected Claude’s recommendations:\n    13\t\n    14\t- **No required password change at first sign-in.** Claude proposed this additional step, but I decided it was unnecessary for our setup. There are approximately eight officers, and a President sets each password face to face. Given the deadline, I did not think another screen was justified. I retained a two-hour idle sign-out because we share a laptop during meetings.\n    15\t- **Only Presidents can publish.** Officers can prepare drafts, but publication requires a President. In the spring, our three sector teams present stock pitches to Kenyon alumni working at William Blair. Material published under the club’s name should therefore be complete and reviewed.\n    16\t- **Only Presidents can manage Pages.** This decision came directly from my sixth WordPress field note, where I found that an Editor could move the About page to the trash. Officers contributing announcements should not also have control over official pages such as Leadership and the Analyst Program.\n    17\t- **Publishing uses a simple confirmation.** Claude suggested displaying a summary of changes before every publish run. I chose a straightforward “Publish this?” confirmation, with the option to unpublish content and run the command again if a correction is needed.\n    18\t- **Pitch writeups credit teams in the body text.** I decided against adding a separate team field. The byline identifies whoever posted the writeup, while the text credits the members who contributed.\n    19\t- **The next meeting appears as a manually edited line on the Homepage.** I chose this over automatic date logic because one of us already updates the email reminder before each meeting. Updating the website can follow the same routine.\n    20\t\n    21\t## 2. Where the AI drifted, and what caught it\n    22\t\n    23\tThe clearest problem was an explicitly requested fix that Claude reported as complete without resolving it. In my T07 prompt, I explained that `scripts/seed_demo.py` would not run with a fresh `.env` file and displayed “Set CMS_ADMIN_PASSWORD and CMS_EDITOR_PASSWORD in .env.” I asked Claude to fix the issue and add a test. It subsequently reported T07 as complete, with all 111 tests passing.\n    24\t\n    25\tHowever, when I ran the seed script myself at approximately 12:20 a.m., it produced the same error and exited, preventing the server from starting. None of the unit tests actually ran the script, which explains why the suite passed. I discovered the problem while manually trying to use the app. I then opened bug issue #9 and addressed it with a test that runs the seed script as a subprocess using a fresh copy of `.env.example`.\n    26\t\n    27\tOther departures from the specification were identified through `/code-review`:\n    28\t\n    29\t- **T01: conflicting glossary files.** The installed skills were newer than those described in the manual and expected a `GLOSSARY.md` file. Although I had already specified in `CLAUDE.md` that the glossary belonged in `CONTEXT.md`, an empty `GLOSSARY.md` and a reference to it in `docs/agents/domain.md` still appeared. The review identified this contradiction, which I corrected in commit `1557b24`. Leaving it unresolved could have caused later tickets to rely on different sources for the project’s vocabulary.\n    30\t- **T06: President self-demotion.** The initial user management implementation allowed a President to demote themselves, despite the specification prohibiting this. With three co-presidents managing accounts, this seemed like a plausible mistake during the spring leadership transition. The review caught it before the commit.\n    31\t- **T05: an addition I retained.** Claude included Pages in the dashboard counts even though the ticket did not request this. I kept the addition because it helps the Presidents identify unpublished pages.\n    32\t\n    33\t## 3. Skills, prompts, and resources\n    34\t\n    35\tI followed the sequence `/grill-with-docs`, `/to-spec`, and `/to-tickets`, which produced seven tickets corresponding to issues #2–#8. I then used `/implement` for each ticket, which invoked `/tdd`, followed by `/code-review`.\n    36\t\n    37\tThe grill was the most useful part of the process. Its 18 questions required me to make specific decisions about how the CMS should serve the club, including the choices described above. The review stage was also valuable because it identified problems in work that `/implement` had already reported as finished.\n    38\t\n    39\tOne source of confusion was the difference between ticket labels and GitHub issue numbers. {"parentUuid":"16943843-064b-4c7c-ac98-ea93ef207aac","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"9acc77cd-1d7b-4777-a4f0-bd06dabcb5ef","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_014unZLFeAZWpgNJ4KCtPfeQ","type":"tool_result","content":"     1\t# IPHS 400 — Mini-Project #2 starter (Web CMS)\n     2\t\n     3\tClick **Use this template** → name your repo **`iphs400-mp2-cms`** → make it **Public**.\n     4\tDo not fork: a fork arrives without an Issues tab, and your tickets live in Issues.\n     5\t\n     6\t## Start here\n     7\t\n     8\t1. `docs/manual_iphs400_mp2-web-cms_20260922.md` — the manual. Read Part 0 and Part 1 first.\n     9\t2. `docs/mp2-grading-rubric_20260922.md` — how you are graded. Read it **before** you build or revise.\n    10\t3. `docs/mp2-setup_context-threshold-hook_20260922.md` — Exercise A, in Part 4 of the manual.\n    11\t\n    12\t## Live URL\n    13\t\n    14\thttps://iaishikb-rgb.github.io/iphs400-mp2-cms/ — the Kenyon College Finance Club public site, served from the `gh-pages` branch.\n    15\t\n    16\t## Run locally\n    17\t\n    18\tNeeds [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and Python 3.12+.\n    19\t\n    20\t```bash\n    21\tuv sync\n    22\tcp .env.example .env                      # demo passwords; change them for anything real\n    23\tuv run python scripts/seed_demo.py        # demo users, club Pages and Posts (safe to re-run)\n    24\tuv run pytest -q                          # optional: run the test suite\n    25\tuv run cms serve                          # admin console at http://localhost:8000/login\n    26\t```\n    27\t\n    28\tDemo sign-ins (from `.env.example`): `admin@example.test` / `change-me-admin` (President, Admin)\n    29\tand `editor@example.test` / `change-me-editor` (Officer, Editor).\n    30\t\n    31\tTo refresh the public site: `uv run cms publish` writes `site/`, and `uv run cms deploy` pushes it\n    32\tto `gh-pages`.\n    33\t\n    34\t## What is here\n    35\t\n    36\t```text\n    37\t.claude/hooks/     the context meter and usage ledger (Exercise A lives in ctx_guard.py)\n    38\tscripts/           usage_report.py (Exercise B lives in spend()), check_submission.py, seed_demo.py\n    39\ttests/             the exercise tests, plus helpers such as client_as(\"editor\")\n    40\tapp/, templates/   the T00 skeleton — every CMS feature is yours to build\n    41\tdocs/adr/          two example decision records\n    42\t```\n    43\t\n    44\tTwo functions are deliberately unfinished and their tests fail until you write them:\n    45\t`decide()` in `.claude/hooks/ctx_guard.py` and `spend()` in `scripts/usage_report.py`.\n    46\tBoth are graded in Stage 2. Use `/tdd`, as the manual says.\n    47\t\n    48\t## Deadlines\n    49\t\n    50\tStage 1 (`mp2-mvp` tag): Tue Sep 29, 2:40 pm Eastern. A preliminary checkpoint, past and ungraded; its 15 points are credited for the tag.\n    51\tStage 2 (`mp2-final` tag): the final, graded submission, due Thu Oct 15, 2:40 pm Eastern, grace until Fri Oct 16, 2:40 pm. The first round (due Oct 6) was graded and returned on Oct 8; the deadline was extended so you can revise after feedback, and one revised `mp2-final` by Oct 15 replaces the earlier grade.\n    52\tMP2plus (optional extra credit): assigned Sun Oct 11, due Tue Oct 20, 2:40 pm Eastern, grace until Wed Oct 21, 2:40 pm. Each exercise is worth 5–10 points, added to your MP2 grade, up to +30.\n    53\tMP2 is graded as a score out of 100, scaled to 5% of the course grade.\n    54\t\n    55\tRun `uv run python scripts/check_submission.py --stage 2` before you submit.\n    56\t\n    57\t## Generative AI Use Statement\n    58\t\n    59\t## Generative AI Use Statement\n    60\t\n    61\tI built this project using Claude Code inside Orca, with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, following the setup we used in class. Claude wrote nearly all of the code. My role was to determine what the club needed, respond to the questions raised during the grill, read the tests and reviews, and identify where the implementation fell short.\n    62\t\n    63\t**Models.** I used Claude Sonnet for most of the project, including the grill, specification, ticket generation, implementation of all seven tickets, and reviews. One early setup session used Haiku because I had not noticed which model was selected. Although my budget plan originally called for opusplan during the planning stages, I switched the grill to Sonnet on the night of October 14 because I was concerned about reaching my five-hour usage limit before beginning implementation.\n    64\t\n    65\t**Skills.** I used the mattpocock skills: `/grill-with-docs`, `/to-spec`, `/to-tickets`, `/implement`, which invoked `/tdd`, and `/code-review`. I also used `/ask-matt` once to check the workflow. Alongside these, I used the course hooks for the context meter, usage ledger, and transcript saver.\n    66\t\n    67\t**Two prompts I sent**\n    68\t\n    69\t1. To begin the grill:\n    70\t\n    71\t   > /grill-with-docs I am building a small CMS for the Kenyon College Finance Club, which my two co-presidents and I run. My field notes are in notes/cms-field-notes.md and my client brief is in notes/client-brief.md. The 7 required capabilities are in docs/manual_iphs400_mp2-web-cms_20260922.md, Part 3.3. Help me decide what they mean for this club. Write the glossary to CONTEXT.md. Ask one question at a time.\n    72\t\n    73\t2. In response to the grill’s proposed sign-in process, at question 14:\n    74\t\n    75\t   > Partly. Yes to signing in with a Kenyon email plus password, and yes to admin-assisted resets. We'd do that in person at a board meeting in Oden anyway. But no forced password change at first sign-in: there are only ~8 officers, a president sets the password face to face, and I'd rather not build an extra screen with the deadline this week. Keep a simple idle sign-out, about 2 hours, because we do share a laptop at meetings.\n    76\t\n    77\t**A model failure.** In my T07 prompt, I explicitly told Claude that `seed_demo.py` would not run with a fresh `.env` file. It displayed the message “Set CMS_ADMIN_PASSWORD and CMS_EDITOR_PASSWORD in .env,” and I asked Claude to fix the problem and add a test. Claude subsequently reported that T07 was complete, with all 111 tests passing. However, when I ran the seed script myself, it produced the same error and exited, leaving the server unable to start.\n    78\t\n    79\tNone of the tests actually ran the seed script, which explains why they passed despite the unresolved problem. I opened bug issue #9 and addressed it in a separate session, this time adding a test that runs the seed script as a subprocess using a fresh copy of `.env.example`. This made me more aware of the limits of a passing test suite: it only establishes that the behavior covered by those tests works. Going forward, I should also use the app myself after each ticket, instead of waiting until the end.\n    80\t\n    81\t**Other issues caught during review.** The `/code-review` skill identified a separate `GLOSSARY.md` created during T01, despite my requirement that the glossary belong in `CONTEXT.md`. It also caught a problem in T06: the initial user management implementation allowed a President to demote themselves, which the specification explicitly prohibited.\n    82\t\n    83\t**Authorship note.** Commits made before October 15 display the placeholder author “Your Full Name” because I had not configured my Git identity on this laptop. The `.mailmap` file maps those commits to me. Every commit in this repository is mine.\n    84\t\n    85\tI drafted this statement with Claude’s help and then edited and rephrased it.\n    86\t\n    87\t### Backends used\n    88\t\n    89\t| Provider | Models | Use |\n    90\t| --- | --- | --- |\n    91\t| Anthropic (Claude Pro) | Sonnet, Haiku | All project development. No backup provider was used. |\n\n#### NOTES\n     1\t# CMS field notes: WordPress Playground\n     2\t\n     3\t**Tuesday, October 13, 2026**\n     4\t\n     5\tI explored WordPress Playground with the Kenyon College Finance Club in mind. I wanted to understand how the system handles publishing and user permissions, but also whether it would be practical for students who are responsible for organizing the club alongside their other commitments. Since our three presidents organize the club and most communication happens through email, the website would need to make information easy to maintain and find.\n     6\t\n     7\t1. **Drafts are not visible on the public site.** I created a sample post titled \"Fall Stock Pitch Night\" and saved it as a draft. When I opened the public site in another tab, the post did not appear. I could only view it through the Preview button while logged in. This is useful for preparing material before it is ready to share, particularly stock pitches that need to be reviewed. However, it also makes a clear distinction between saving and publishing necessary: an officer could save an announcement and assume members can already see it. The title was just for testing; our actual stock pitch competition takes place in the spring.\n     8\t\n     9\t2. **Publishing requires an additional confirmation.** Clicking Publish first opened a panel asking me to confirm that the post was ready. Although this adds another step, I can see why it is useful. For our club, accidentally publishing an unfinished pitch could affect how alumni perceive the work we do. The confirmation gives the person posting a chance to check the material before it becomes public.\n    10\t\n    11\t3. **Pages and posts serve different purposes.** In my test, the About page appeared in the site's menu, while the post appeared in the blog feed. This helped clarify how we could organize the club's website. Pages would hold information that remains relevant over time, such as About, Leadership, and the Analyst Program. Posts would hold dated material, including meeting announcements, event recaps, and stock pitch writeups. Our current Wix site relies on static pages, which makes it harder to distinguish current activity from general club information.\n    12\t\n    13\t4. **The URL slug is generated automatically, but its settings are easy to miss.** WordPress created the slug \"fall-stock-pitch-night\" from my post's title. I only found the setting after opening the post settings sidebar. I do not think most officers would look for it unless they needed to change the URL. Automatic generation would therefore be helpful, and for our own system I would want shared links to remain reliable even if someone later edits a title.\n    14\t\n    15\t5. **Restrictions are enforced beyond the navigation menu.** I created an Editor account and logged in with it. The Users menu was absent from the sidebar. When I entered /wp-admin/users.php directly in the address bar, WordPress displayed, \"Sorry, you are not allowed to list users.\" This showed that the restriction was enforced by the system itself. For our website, account management should be limited to the three presidents, and those limits should still apply if someone tries to reach the page directly.\n    16\t\n    17\t6. **The Editor role allows more control than our officers would need.** While logged in as an Editor, I could edit and move other people's pages to the trash, including the About page. This would be a concern for the club because officers contributing announcements or writeups should not also be able to delete the Leadership or Analyst Program pages. WordPress's default Editor role therefore does not match the permissions we want. Our system would need to restrict access to these pages more specifically.\n    18\t\n    19\t7. **The post status filters make unfinished work easy to find.** The All Posts screen displayed links for All, Published, and Drafts, with a count beside each. Clicking Drafts showed the posts that had not yet been published. This would be useful when the presidents are reviewing announcements or stock pitch writeups. It makes it easier to see what still needs attention without opening every post individually.\n    20\t\n    21\t8. **The block editor offers more options than our everyday updates require.** Each paragraph is treated as a separate block, and the add menu includes many different types of content. These options may be useful for a more elaborate website, but most club updates would only need a title, text, and a few links. For announcements about our meetings every other week in Oden 110, or links to resume review forms, a simpler editor would likely be easier to use. Plain Markdown could be sufficient for much of this work.\n#### CTX\n     1\t# CONTEXT.md glossary\n     2\t\n     3\tProject vocabulary for the Kenyon College Finance Club (KCFC) website. One word per concept; if a better word appears, change it here.\n     4\t\n     5\t## People and roles\n     6\t\n     7\t**President**: One of the three students who run KCFC. Every President holds the Admin role.\n     8\t\n     9\t**Officer**: A club member other than a President who helps run the club. Every Officer holds the Editor role while in office.\n    10\t\n    11\t**Admin**: The role held by the three Presidents. Can create, edit, publish and delete Posts and Pages, and manage Users.\n    12\t\n    13\t**Editor**: The role held by Officers. Can create and edit Posts and save them as Drafts. Cannot publish, cannot delete a published Post, cannot touch Pages, and cannot see User management. An Editor sees and edits only their own Posts, so a sector team's writeup changes only through its own author until a President reviews it. Admins see and edit every Post.\n    14\t\n    15\t**User**: Anyone with an individual account on the admin console. Only Presidents and Officers are Users. Never shared between people.\n    16\t\n    17\t**Visitor**: Anyone reading the public site: prospective members, current members, alumni, recruiters. Visitors never log in, and everything on the public site is visible to all of them. There is no members-only content.\n    18\t\n    19\t**Sign-in**: A User signs in with their Kenyon email address and a password. A President creates the account and sets the first password face to face; there is no forced change at first sign-in. A lost password is reset by an Admin in person, never by email.\n    20\t\n    21\t**Idle sign-out**: A User is signed out automatically after about 2 hours without activity, because the Club laptop is shared at meetings.\n    22\t\n    23\t**Display name**: The name a User is known by publicly, e.g. \"Kim Lee\". A President sets it when creating the User and can edit it later. It is the only name used in a Byline; the email address is never shown.\n    24\t\n    25\t**Deactivated**: A User switched off by an Admin when their time in office ends. They can no longer sign in, and any open session ends at their next action. Their Posts keep their name as author. An Admin can reactivate them. Users are never deleted. No backup provider was used. |\n\n#### NOTES\n     1\t# CMS field notes: WordPress Playground\n     2\t\n     3\t**Tuesday, October 13, 2026**\n     4\t\n     5\tI explored WordPress Playground with the Kenyon College Finance Club in mind. I wanted to understand how the system handles publishing and user permissions, but also whether it would be practical for students who are responsible for organizing the club alongside their other commitments. Since our three presidents organize the club and most communication happens through email, the website would need to make information easy to maintain and find.\n     6\t\n     7\t1. **Drafts are not visible on the public site.** I created a sample post titled \"Fall Stock Pitch Night\" and saved it as a draft. When I opened the public site in another tab, the post did not appear. I could only view it through the Preview button while logged in. This is useful for preparing material before it is ready to share, particularly stock pitches that need to be reviewed. However, it also makes a clear distinction between saving and publishing necessary: an officer could save an announcement and assume members can already see it. The title was just for testing; our actual stock pitch competition takes place in the spring.\n     8\t\n     9\t2. **Publishing requires an additional confirmation.** Clicking Publish first opened a panel asking me to confirm that the post was ready. Although this adds another step, I can see why it is useful. For our club, accidentally publishing an unfinished pitch could affect how alumni perceive the work we do. The confirmation gives the person posting a chance to check the material before it becomes public.\n    10\t\n    11\t3. **Pages and posts serve different purposes.** In my test, the About page appeared in the site's menu, while the post appeared in the blog feed. This helped clarify how we could organize the club's website. Pages would hold information that remains relevant over time, such as About, Leadership, and the Analyst Program. Posts would hold dated material, including meeting announcements, event recaps, and stock pitch writeups. Our current Wix site relies on static pages, which makes it harder to distinguish current activity from general club information.\n    12\t\n    13\t4. **The URL slug is generated automatically, but its settings are easy to miss.** WordPress created the slug \"fall-stock-pitch-night\" from my post's title. I only found the setting after opening the post settings sidebar. I do not think most officers would look for it unless they needed to change the URL. Automatic generation would therefore be helpful, and for our own system I would want shared links to remain reliable even if someone later edits a title.\n    14\t\n    15\t5. **Restrictions are enforced beyond the navigation menu.** I created an Editor account and logged in with it. The Users menu was absent from the sidebar. When I entered /wp-admin/users.php directly in the address bar, WordPress displayed, \"Sorry, you are not allowed to list users.\" This showed that the restriction was enforced by the system itself. For our website, account management should be limited to the three presidents, and those limits should still apply if someone tries to reach the page directly.\n    16\t\n    17\t6. **The Editor role allows more control than our officers would need.** While logged in as an Editor, I could edit and move other people's pages to the trash, including the About page. This would be a concern for the club because officers contributing announcements or writeups should not also be able to delete the Leadership or Analyst Program pages. WordPress's default Editor role therefore does not match the permissions we want. Our system would need to restrict access to these pages more specifically.\n    18\t\n    19\t7. **The post status filters make unfinished work easy to find.** The All Posts screen displayed links for All, Published, and Drafts, with a count beside each. Clicking Drafts showed the posts that had not yet been published. This would be useful when the presidents are reviewing announcements or stock pitch writeups. It makes it easier to see what still needs attention without opening every post individually.\n    20\t\n    21\t8. **The block editor offers more options than our everyday updates require.** Each paragraph is treated as a separate block, and the add menu includes many different types of content. These options may be useful for a more elaborate website, but most club updates would only need a title, text, and a few links. For announcements about our meetings every other week in Oden 110, or links to resume review forms, a simpler editor would likely be easier to use. Plain Markdown could be sufficient for much of this work.\n#### CTX\n     1\t# CONTEXT.md glossary\n     2\t\n     3\tProject vocabulary for the Kenyon College Finance Club (KCFC) website. local markdown is also supported out of the box)\\n- **Triage labels**: the strings used for the five canonical triage roles\\n- **Domain docs**: where `GLOSSARY.md` and ADRs live, and the consumer rules for reading them\\n\\nThis is a prompt-driven skill, not a deterministic script. Explore, present what you found, confirm with the user, then write.\\n\\n## Process\\n\\n### 1. Explore\\n\\nLook at the current repo to understand its starting state. Read whatever exists; don't assume:\\n\\n- `git remote -v` and `.git/config`: is this a GitHub repo? Which one?\\n- `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` at the repo root: does either exist? Is there already an `## Agent skills` section in either?\\n- `GLOSSARY.md` and `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` at the repo root\\n- `docs/adr/` and any `src/*/docs/adr/` directories\\n- `docs/agents/`: does this skill's prior output already exist?\\n- `.scratch/`: a sign that a local-markdown issue tracker convention is already in use\\n- Is the `triage` skill installed? (a `triage` skill folder alongside this one, or `triage` in your available skills.) This decides whether Section B runs at all.\\n- Monorepo signals: a `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, a `workspaces` field in `package.json`, or a populated `packages/*` with its own `src/`. These are present only in a genuinely large multi-package repo; their absence means single-context, which is almost every repo.\\n\\n### 2. Present findings and ask\\n\\nSummarise what's present and what's missing. Then take the sections in order. One section, one answer, then the next.\\n\\nLead each section with the recommended answer so the user can accept it in a word. Give a one-line explainer only when the choice genuinely branches; skip the section entirely when exploration already settled it (Section B when `triage` isn't installed, Section C when there's no monorepo).\\n\\n**Section A: Issue tracker.**\\n\\n> Explainer: The \\\"issue tracker\\\" is where issues live for this repo. Skills like `to-tickets`, `triage`, and `to-spec` read from and write to it. They need to know whether to call `gh issue create`, write a markdown file under `.scratch/`, or follow some other workflow you describe. Pick the place you actually track work for this repo.\\n\\nDefault posture: these skills were designed for GitHub. If a `git remote` points at GitHub, propose that. If a `git remote` points at GitLab (`gitlab.com` or a self-hosted host), propose GitLab. Otherwise (or if the user prefers), offer:\\n\\n- **GitHub**: issues live in the repo's GitHub Issues (uses the `gh` CLI)\\n- **GitLab**: issues live in the repo's GitLab Issues (uses the [`glab`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cli) CLI)\\n- **Local markdown**: issues live as files under `.scratch/<feature>/` in this repo (good for solo projects or repos without a remote)\\n- **Other** (Jira, Linear, etc.): ask the user to describe the workflow in one paragraph; the skill will record it as freeform prose\\n\\nRecord the choice in `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`. The GitHub and GitLab templates carry a \\\"PRs as a request surface\\\" flag, defaulted **off**. Leave it off and don't raise it: a user who wants external PRs in the triage queue can flip the flag in the file later.\\n\\n**Section B: Triage label vocabulary.** Skip this section entirely if the `triage` skill isn't installed (exploration told you), since an uninstalled skill needs no labels.\\n\\nIf it is installed, ask exactly one question:\\n\\n> Do you want to keep the default triage labels? (recommended: **yes**)\\n\\nThe defaults are the five canonical roles, each label string equal to its name: `needs-triage`, `needs-info`, `ready-for-agent`, `ready-for-human`, `wontfix`. On **yes**, write them as-is. Only if the user says no, usually because their tracker already uses other names (e.g. `bug:triage` for `needs-triage`), collect the overrides so `triage` applies existing labels instead of creating duplicates.\\n\\n**Section C: Domain docs.** Default to **single-context** (one `GLOSSARY.md` + `docs/adr/` at the repo root). This fits almost every repo; write it without asking.\\n\\nOffer **multi-context** (a root `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` pointing to per-context `GLOSSARY.md` files) only when exploration found monorepo signals. Then confirm which layout they want.\\n\\n### 3. Confirm and edit\\n\\nShow the user a draft of:\\n\\n- The `## Agent skills` block to add to whichever of `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` is being edited (see step 4 for selection rules)\\n- The contents of `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`, `docs/agents/domain.md`, and `docs/agents/triage-labels.md` (the last only when `triage` is installed)\\n\\nLet them edit before writing.\\n\\n### 4. Write\\n\\n**Pick the file to edit:**\\n\\n- If `CLAUDE.md` exists, edit it.\\n- Else if `AGENTS.md` exists, edit it.\\n- If neither exists, ask the user which one to create; don't pick for them.\\n\\nNever create `AGENTS.md` when `CLAUDE.md` already exists (or vice versa); always edit the one that's already there.\\n\\nIf an `## Agent skills` block already exists in the chosen file, update its contents in-place rather than appending a duplicate. Don't overwrite user edits to the surrounding sections.\\n\\nThe block:\\n\\n```markdown\\n## Agent skills\\n\\n### Issue tracker\\n\\n[one-line summary of where issues are tracked]. See `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.\\n\\n### Triage labels\\n\\n[one-line summary of the label vocabulary]. See `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`.\\n\\n### Domain docs\\n\\n[one-line summary of layout: \\\"single-context\\\" or \\\"multi-context\\\"]. See `docs/agents/domain.md`.\\n```\\n\\nInclude the `### Triage labels` sub-block, and write `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`, only when `triage` is installed and Section B ran. When it isn't, both are omitted.\\n\\nWhen Section B ran on GitHub or GitLab, create each configured label the tracker lacks (`gh label create` / `glab label create`).\\n\\nThen write the docs files using the seed templates in this skill folder as a starting point:\\n\\n- [issue-tracker-github.md](./issue-tracker-github.md): GitHub issue tracker\\n- [issue-tracker-gitlab.md](./issue-tracker-gitlab.md): GitLab issue tracker\\n- [issue-tracker-local.md](./issue-tracker-local.md): local-markdown issue tracker\\n- [triage-labels.md](./triage-labels.md): label mapping (only if `triage` is installed)\\n- [domain.md](./domain.md): domain doc consumer rules + layout\\n\\nFor \\\"other\\\" issue trackers, write `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` from scratch using the user's description.\\n\\n### 5. Done\\n\\nTell the user the setup is complete and which engineering skills will now read from these files. Mention they can edit `docs/agents/*.md` directly later; re-running this skill is only necessary if they want to switch issue trackers or restart from scratch.\\n\"}]},\"isMeta\":true,\"turnCompanion\":true,\"uuid\":\"796f3134-b882-4b7f-b663-f9d6c406c435\",\"timestamp\":\"2026-10-14T02:16:41.836Z\",\"userType\":\"external\",\"entrypoint\":\"cli\",\"cwd\":\"/Users/biswas1/code/iphs400-mp2-cms\",\"sessionId\":\"50d5de93-5101-40c3-9b1e-562452c3dac4\",\"version\":\"2.1.285\",\"gitBranch\":\"main\"}\n{\"parentUuid\":\"796f3134-b882-4b7f-b663-f9d6c406c435\",\"isSidechain\":false,\"attachment\":{\"type\":\"environment\",\"snapshot\":{\"workingDirectory\":\"/Users/biswas1/code/iphs400-mp2-cms\",\"isWorktree\":false,\"isGitRepo\":true,\"additionalWorkingDirectories\":[],\"platform\":\"darwin\",\"shell\":\"zsh\",\"osVersion\":\"Darwin 25.5.0\"}},\"type\":\"attachment\",\"uuid\":\"332e8177-1ce8-4360-82f4-7d6d80718d28\",\"timestamp\":\"2026-10-14T02:16:41.835Z\",\"rendered\":[{\"content\":\"<system-reminder>\\n# Environment\\nYou have been invoked in the following environment: \\n - Primary working directory: /Users/biswas1/code/iphs400-mp2-cms\\n - Is a git repository: true\\n - Platform: darwin\\n - Shell: zsh\\n - OS Version: Darwin 25.5.0\\n</system-reminder>\"}],\"renderedRole\":\"system\",\"userType\":\"external\",\"entrypoint\":\"cli\",\"cwd\":\"/Users/biswas1/code/iphs400-mp2-cms\",\"sessionId\":\"50d5de93-5101-40c3-9b1e-562452c3dac4\",\"version\":\"2.1.285\",\"gitBranch\":\"main\"}\n{\"parentUuid\":\"332e8177-1ce8-4360-82f4-7d6d80718d28\",\"isSidechain\":false,\"attachment\":{\"type\":\"model\",\"identity\":{\"modelId\":\"claude-haiku-4-5-20251001\",\"marketingName\":\"Haiku 4.5\",\"knowledgeCutoff\":\"February 2025\"},\"text\":\"You are powered by the model named Haiku 4.5. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.\n19\t\n20\tWork the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.\n21\t\n22\tFormat a round like so:\n23\t\n24\t```\n25\t❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>\n26\t\n27\t➡️ <your recommended answer>\n28\t\n29\t---\n30\t\n31\t❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>\n32\t\n33\t➡️ <your recommended answer>\n34\t```\n35\t\n36\tWord each question so \"yes\" accepts your recommended answer.\n37\t\n38\tEach round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.\n39\t\n40\tFinding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.\n41\t\n42\tThe session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.\n43\t\n44\t\n45\t--- L36 USER 2026-10-15T02:33:02.761Z\n46\tBase directory for this skill: /Users/biswas1/code/iphs400-mp2-cms/.claude/skills/domain-modeling\n47\t\n48\t# Domain Modeling\n49\t\n50\tActively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)\n51\t\n52\t## File structure\n53\t\n54\tMost repos have a single context:\n55\t\n56\t```\n57\t/\n58\t├── GLOSSARY.md\n59\t├── docs/\n60\t│   └── adr/\n61\t│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md\n62\t│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md\n63\t└── src/\n64\t```\n65\t\n66\tIf a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:\n67\t\n68\t```\n69\t/\n70\t├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md\n71\t├── docs/\n72\t│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions\n73\t├── src/\n74\t│   ├── ordering/\n75\t│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md\n76\t│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions\n77\t│   └── billing/\n78\t│       ├── GLOSSARY.md\n79\t│       └── docs/adr/\n80\t```\n81\t\n82\tCreate files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.\n83\t\n84\t## During the session\n85\t\n86\t### Challenge against the glossary\n87\t\n88\tWhen the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. \"Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?\"\n89\t\n90\t### Sharpen fuzzy language\n91\t\n92\tWhen the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. \"You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things.\"\n93\t\n94\t### Discuss concrete scenarios\n95\t\n96\tWhen domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.\n97\t\n98\t### Cross-reference with code\n99\t\n100\tWhen the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: \"Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?\"\n101\t\n102\t### Update GLOSSARY.md inline\n103\t\n104\tWhen a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).\n105\t\n106\t`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.\n107\t\n108\t### Offer ADRs sparingly\n109\t\n110\tOnly offer to create an ADR when all three are true:\n111\t\n112\t1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful\n113\t2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder \"why did they do it this way?\"\n114\t3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons\n115\t\n116\tIf any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.\n19\t\n20\tWork the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.\n21\t\n22\tFormat a round like so:\n23\t\n24\t```\n25\t❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>\n26\t\n27\t➡️ <your recommended answer>\n28\t\n29\t---\n30\t\n31\t❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>\n32\t\n33\t➡️ <your recommended answer>\n34\t```\n35\t\n36\tWord each question so \"yes\" accepts your recommended answer.\n37\t\n38\tEach round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.\n39\t\n40\tFinding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.\n41\t\n42\tThe session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.\n43\t\n44\t\n45\t--- L36 USER 2026-10-15T02:33:02.761Z\n46\tBase directory for this skill: /Users/biswas1/code/iphs400-mp2-cms/.claude/skills/domain-modeling\n47\t\n48\t# Domain Modeling\n49\t\n50\tActively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)\n51\t\n52\t## File structure\n53\t\n54\tMost repos have a single context:\n55\t\n56\t```\n57\t/\n58\t├── GLOSSARY.md\n59\t├── docs/\n60\t│   └── adr/\n61\t│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md\n62\t│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md\n63\t└── src/\n64\t```\n65\t\n66\tIf a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:\n67\t\n68\t```\n69\t/\n70\t├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md\n71\t├── docs/\n72\t│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions\n73\t├── src/\n74\t│   ├── ordering/\n75\t│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md\n76\t│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions\n77\t│   └── billing/\n78\t│       ├── GLOSSARY.md\n79\t│       └── docs/adr/\n80\t```\n81\t\n82\tCreate files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.\n83\t\n84\t## During the session\n85\t\n86\t### Challenge against the glossary\n87\t\n88\tWhen the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. \"Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?\"\n89\t\n90\t### Sharpen fuzzy language\n91\t\n92\tWhen the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. \"You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things.\"\n93\t\n94\t### Discuss concrete scenarios\n95\t\n96\tWhen domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.\n97\t\n98\t### Cross-reference with code\n99\t\n100\tWhen the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: \"Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?\"\n101\t\n102\t### Update GLOSSARY.md inline\n103\t\n104\tWhen a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).\n105\t\n106\t`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.\n107\t\n108\t### Offer ADRs sparingly\n109\t\n110\tOnly offer to create an ADR when all three are true:\n111\t\n112\t1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful\n113\t2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder \"why did they do it this way?\"\n114\t3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons\n115\t\n116\tIf any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.\n\nWork the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.\n\nFormat a round like so:\n\n```\n❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>\n\n➡️ <your recommended answer>\n\n---\n\n❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>\n\n➡️ <your recommended answer>\n```\n\nWord each question so \"yes\" accepts your recommended answer.\n\nEach round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.\n\nFinding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.\n\n\n--- L36 USER 2026-10-15T02:33:02.761Z\nBase directory for this skill: /Users/biswas1/code/iphs400-mp2-cms/.claude/skills/domain-modeling\n\n# Domain Modeling\n\nActively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)\n\n## File structure\n\nMost repos have a single context:\n\n```\n/\n├── GLOSSARY.md\n├── docs/\n│   └── adr/\n│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md\n│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md\n└── src/\n```\n\nIf a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:\n\n```\n/\n├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md\n├── docs/\n│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions\n├── src/\n│   ├── ordering/\n│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md\n│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions\n│   └── billing/\n│       ├── GLOSSARY.md\n│       └── docs/adr/\n```\n\nCreate files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.\n\n## During the session\n\n### Challenge against the glossary\n\nWhen the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. \"Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?\"\n\n### Sharpen fuzzy language\n\nWhen the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. \"You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things.\"\n\n### Discuss concrete scenarios\n\nWhen domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.\n\n### Cross-reference with code\n\nWhen the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: \"Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?\"\n\n### Update GLOSSARY.md inline\n\nWhen a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).\n\n`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.\n\n### Offer ADRs sparingly\n\nOnly offer to create an ADR when all three are true:\n\n1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful\n2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder \"why did they do it this way?\"\n3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons\n\nIf any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. {"type":"api-request-blob","sessionId":"9c18cc4d-d420-4c1a-83a4-349b624f72ef","hash":"63635ce850838eeaa7a3bb1306e81d7266bbab64c6b61e6d98adbd2f110bc6d5","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_012wa1XE7Di2eJPxAiBLFLaE","type":"tool_result","content":"\"\"\"The `cms` command: serve, publish, deploy.\n\n    uv run cms serve      # admin console + public preview at http://localhost:8000\n    uv run cms publish    # render site/ from published content\n    uv run cms deploy     # push site/ to the gh-pages branch (Pages serves it)\n\"\"\"\nfrom __future__ import annotations\n\nimport argparse\nimport subprocess\nimport sys\n\nfrom app import settings\nfrom app.publish import publish\n\n\ndef main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:\n    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog=\"cms\")\n    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest=\"command\", required=True)\n    serve = sub.add_parser(\"serve\", help=\"run the admin console locally\")\n    serve.add_argument(\"--port\", type=int, default=8000)\n    serve.add_argument(\"--reload\", action=\"store_true\", default=True)\n    sub.add_parser(\"publish\", help=\"render site/ from published content\")\n    deploy = sub.add_parser(\"deploy\", help=\"push site/ to gh-pages\")\n    deploy.add_argument(\"--message\", default=\"Publish site\")\n    args = parser.parse_args(argv)\n\n    if args.command == \"serve\":\n        try:\n            settings.require_safe_secret_key()\n        except RuntimeError as problem:\n            print(problem)\n            return 1\n        import uvicorn\n\n        uvicorn.run(\"app.main:app\", port=args.port, reload=args.reload)\n        return 0\n\n    if args.command == \"publish\":\n        out = publish()\n        print(f\"Wrote {out}. Preview it with:  python3 -m http.server -d {out} 8001\")\n        return 0\n\n    if args.command == \"deploy\":\n        if not settings.SITE.exists():\n            print(\"site/ does not exist yet — run `uv run cms publish` first.\")\n            return 1\n        result = subprocess.run(\n            [sys.executable, \"-m\", \"ghp_import\", \"-n\", \"-p\", \"-m\", args.message,\n             str(settings.SITE)],\n        )\n        if result.returncode == 0:\n            print(\"Pushed to gh-pages. Settings -> Pages -> Deploy from a branch -> \"\n                  \"gh-pages / root, then wait up to 10 minutes.\")\n        return result.returncode\n    return 1\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    raise SystemExit(main())\n6:dependencies = [\n7-    \"fastapi>=0.115\",\n8-    \"uvicorn[standard]>=0.32\",\n9-    \"jinja2>=3.1\",\nShell cwd was reset to /Users/biswas1/code/iphs400-mp2-cms","is_error":false}]}}
